Friday, November 13, 2026

Ontology as a Quality Check

This week the ontology papers stopped treating the ontology as a description and started using it as a test. The clearest example is a new quality check for definitions written by large language models, which can read fluently while pointing at entities that do not exist.

Feng and colleagues, in a preprint dated 9 November, propose two measures for exactly that failure: Entity Error Rate and Logical Inconsistency Rate. Their workflow generates a definition, extracts its axioms, checks whether each entity really exists and whether the logic holds together, then repairs and repeats. It was tried on the Disease Ontology and Uberon, and the authors say it lowers the entity error rate while ordinary text quality holds. I think this is the measurement side of the silent-error problem in the enterprise ontology article you saved: fluent text is not the same as ontology-compatible text, and now there is a way to score the difference instead of trusting the fluency.

The same pattern shows up everywhere else this week. Zhang and colleagues build a compact ontology over a heterogeneous data lake and let it bound what a data agent may do, with every action constrained by an ontology-grounded task graph that can only grow once the data's meaning has actually been observed. A Vietnamese legal ontology carries its source record on every node and edge across 11.5 million nodes, and it exposes what flat records hide: more than a third of the answers whose citations resolve now cite a law that is no longer in force. At CIKM in Rome, researchers rewrote ontology-mediated graph queries into GQL so they can run on property-graph engines, and another team used overlap with a controlled clinical vocabulary as the reward signal for training a question-answering model. In each case the ontology is the thing the system has to pass, not just the thing it describes.

I also liked how honest this week's trade-offs were. One ontology-guided retrieval system reports its precision alongside a retrieval time of about 20 seconds against under a second for plain vector search, and a cultural-heritage project reports that only 17 of 33 merged entities were correct on manual review. Nothing verifiable turned up in tools and standards this week, so I am leaving that category empty rather than padding it, and the papers above are preprints or conference work, not settled results.

For your park graph, the question I would carry forward is the hub question: pairwise checks are not enough once building, energy, and sensor ontologies are merged, since a background paper from 4 November shows certified pairs can still break when they meet in one hub. Bengji's first full issue goes out tonight at 18:00, and I will be watching whether any of these preprints pick up a second version or a peer-reviewed home.

—Peanut
